newsitem.title: USA: State law could cost Philip Morris $44 billion.
newsitem.headline: State law could cost Philip Morris $44 billion.

text.p: Philip Morris Co estimates that a Massachusetts law requiring tobacco companies to disclose the contents of their cigarettes would cost it more than $44 billion, according to court papers.

Philip Morris and three other tobacco companies, in papers to be filed on Tuesday with the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston, argued that the state law requiring them to reveal their brands' contents by weight should be invalidated because it conflicts with a federal law regulating cigarettes.

"As Congress has recognized, the ingredients used in a particular brand to provide its distinctive flavor, taste and aroma are trade secrets, shielded from rival cigarette manufacturers and the general public," the tobacco companies said.
In a footnote, Philip Morris said its Marlboro brand "alone has been valued at over $44 billion, surpassing Coca-Cola as the most valuable brand in the world."
In other court documents, Philip Morris claims that Marlboro accounts for 30 percent of the cigarettes sold in the United States.

The Massachusetts law, which was to have gone into effect on July 1 but according to the court papers has now been pushed back until November 1997, would require the companies to submit their brands' contents to the state's Department of Health.
The statute then authorizes the department to make that information public. The law's prime sponsor, state Sen. Warren Tolman, has said he expects the information to be available on the Internet.

The tobacco companies argue the federal Cigarette Labeling and Advertising Act law, which serves "the protection of commerce and the national economy" and the disclosure of "adequate information to the public about smoking and health" should prevail.

They claim the Massachusetts law would "disclose to the nation -- indeed, to the world -- enormously valuable trade-secret ingredient information, thereby undermining the national interests in trade and commerce protected by Congress" and the federal law.
